nameStory: The charming name "Aunt Lucy" remains a bit of a botanical mystery, with no clear documentation of who the original Lucy was or why this modest wildflower bears her name. Perhaps some long-ago botanist or gardener had a beloved Aunt Lucy who reminded them of this unassuming but reliable little plant. The more formal name Ellisia honors John Ellis, an 18th-century British naturalist who corresponded with the famous Carl Linnaeus.
description: Aunt Lucy is a small, delicate annual wildflower that's quite rare in New England, belonging to the borage family. This low-growing plant typically reaches just 6-12 inches tall with soft, somewhat hairy stems and leaves. It produces tiny, inconspicuous flowers that are easy to overlook among other vegetation. Despite its modest appearance, it's a fascinating native plant that few people ever encounter in the wild.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white to pale blue flowers, usually less than 1/4 inch across, that close up during the day and open in evening or on cloudy days - hence the species name 'nyctelea' meaning night-closing

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, deeply lobed leaves that feel slightly fuzzy to the touch, arranged alternately along the stem with an almost ferny appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, sprawling annual that forms small patches, often looking somewhat weedy or unassuming among other spring vegetation

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small capsules that split open to reveal dark seeds, giving it the alternate name 'waterpod' due to the capsule's shape

habitat: Aunt Lucy prefers moist, rich soils in partially shaded areas such as woodland edges, stream banks, and disturbed ground in wooded areas. Given its extreme rarity in New England with only one recorded observation, it likely occurs in very specific microhabitats that meet its particular needs. It's more common in the Midwest and western North America, so any New England sighting would be quite special.

seasonality.spring: Emerges early in spring and begins blooming in late spring, when the soft, lobed leaves are most visible before other vegetation fills in.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming through early summer, though flowers are most noticeable in evening hours when they open. Seeds develop and ripen during mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Plant dies back after setting seed, leaving little trace above ground as it completes its annual cycle.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence, existing only as seeds in the soil waiting for the next growing season.

funFact: Aunt Lucy is essentially a botanical night owl - its tiny flowers actually close during bright daylight and open in the evening or on cloudy days, making it one of the few wildflowers that's literally easier to see on a gray, overcast day than in full sunshine!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded sighting in New England, Aunt Lucy is more likely to be overlooked entirely than confused with other plants. Its small size and inconspicuous flowers might cause it to be dismissed as a young weed or unidentified seedling rather than recognized as a distinct wildflower species.
contextualKnowledge: There's some taxonomic confusion around Aunt Lucy - some sources place it in the waterleaf family (Hydrophyllaceae) while others put it in the borage family (Boraginaceae), reflecting ongoing botanical research into plant relationships. This uncertainty doesn't affect field identification but shows how plant classification continues to evolve with new scientific understanding.
compareHints: Aunt Lucy is the only species in its genus Ellisia, making it unique among New England plants. Within the borage family, it's much smaller and more delicate than familiar relatives like comfrey or borage itself. Its night-closing flowers and deeply lobed leaves distinguish it from other small borage family members like forget-me-nots, which have simpler leaves and flowers that stay open during the day.
